## 1. Load Datasets

Python: `pd.read_csv()` → R: `read.csv()`

```{r}
dfc <- read.csv("calories.csv")
dfe <- read.csv("exercise.csv")

head(dfc, 5)
head(dfe, 5)
```

## 2. Merge the Two Datasets

Python: `pd.merge(dfc, dfe, on='User_ID')` → R: `merge(..., by = "User_ID")`

```{r}
df <- merge(dfc, dfe, by = "User_ID")

head(df, 5)
```

## 3. Dataset Overview

Python: `df.shape` → `dim()`, `df.info()` → `str()`

```{r}
dim(df)
str(df)
```

## 4. Drop the User_ID Column

Python: `df.drop(['User_ID'], axis=1)` → R: assign `NULL` to the column

```{r}
df$User_ID <- NULL

head(df, 3)
```

## 5. Missing Values

Python: `df.isnull().sum()` → R: `colSums(is.na(df))`

```{r}
colSums(is.na(df))
```

## 6. Summary Statistics

Python: `df.describe()` → R: `summary()`

```{r}
summary(df)
```

## 7. Distribution and Boxplot of Each Variable

Python: `sns.histplot()` + `sns.boxplot()` → R: `hist()` + `boxplot()`

`par(mfrow = c(7, 2))` makes a grid with 7 rows and 2 columns, like `plt.subplots(7, 2)`.

```{r fig.height=28, fig.width=10}
columns <- c("Calories", "Age", "Height", "Weight",
             "Duration", "Heart_Rate", "Body_Temp")

par(mfrow = c(7, 2))

for (column in columns) {
  # Histogram with a density curve (like kde=True)
  hist(df[[column]],
       freq = FALSE,
       main = paste("Distribution of", column),
       xlab = column)
  lines(density(df[[column]]))

  # Horizontal boxplot
  boxplot(df[[column]],
          horizontal = TRUE,
          main = paste("Boxplot of", column),
          xlab = column)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))   # reset the plotting area
```

## 8. Remove Outliers (IQR Method)

Python loops over each column and keeps only the rows inside the IQR limits.
The same idea in R uses a `for` loop and row filtering with `df[condition, ]`.

```{r}
cat("Rows before removing outliers:", nrow(df), "\n")

for (column in columns) {
  q1  <- quantile(df[[column]], 0.25)
  q3  <- quantile(df[[column]], 0.75)
  iqr <- q3 - q1

  low  <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
  high <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

  df <- df[df[[column]] >= low & df[[column]] <= high, ]
}

cat("Rows after removing outliers: ", nrow(df), "\n")
```

## 9. Log Transformation of Age

Python: `np.log1p()` → R: `log1p()` (built in)

```{r}
df$Age <- log1p(df$Age)
```

## 10. Distributions After Cleaning

Same plots as Step 7, to compare before and after.

```{r fig.height=28, fig.width=10}
par(mfrow = c(7, 2))

for (column in columns) {
  hist(df[[column]],
       freq = FALSE,
       main = paste("Distribution of", column),
       xlab = column)
  lines(density(df[[column]]))

  boxplot(df[[column]],
          horizontal = TRUE,
          main = paste("Boxplot of", column),
          xlab = column)
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

## 11. Encode the Categorical Variable (Gender)

Python: `pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['Gender'], drop_first=True)`

In R, the same result comes from `ifelse()`: `female` becomes the reference group (0)
and `male` becomes 1. Then the original `Gender` column is removed.

```{r}
df$Gender_male <- ifelse(df$Gender == "male", 1, 0)
df$Gender <- NULL

head(df, 3)
```

## 12. Correlation

Python: `df.corr()` + `sns.heatmap()` → R: `cor()`

```{r}
round(cor(df), 2)
```

Optional heatmap (base R, not covered in class yet):

```{r fig.height=6, fig.width=7}
heatmap(cor(df), Rowv = NA, Colv = NA, symm = TRUE, margins = c(9, 9))
```

## 13. Separate Features (x) and Target (y)

Python: `df.drop('Calories', axis=1)` and `df['Calories']`

```{r}
x <- df[, names(df) != "Calories"]
y <- df$Calories
```

## 14. Train/Test Split (80% / 20%)

Python: `train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)`

`set.seed(42)` makes the random split reproducible. R's random generator is different from
Python's, so the exact rows chosen will not match your Python split.

```{r}
set.seed(42)

n <- nrow(df)
train_index <- sample(1:n, size = floor(0.8 * n))

xtrain <- x[train_index, ]
xtest  <- x[-train_index, ]
ytrain <- y[train_index]
ytest  <- y[-train_index]

cat("Training rows:", nrow(xtrain), "\n")
cat("Testing rows: ", nrow(xtest), "\n")
```

## 15. Standardization

Python: `StandardScaler()` with `fit_transform(xtrain)` and `transform(xtest)`

`scale()` does the standardization (z-score), as in the Standardization lesson.
The mean and standard deviation come from the **training** data only and are then
reused on the test data, so no information leaks from test to train.

```{r}
xtrain_scaled <- scale(xtrain)

xtest_scaled <- scale(xtest,
                      center = attr(xtrain_scaled, "scaled:center"),
                      scale  = attr(xtrain_scaled, "scaled:scale"))

head(xtrain_scaled, 3)
head(xtest_scaled, 3)
```

The data is now fully preprocessed and ready for modeling.
